title: Not even Zeus
hookLine: "I'll chain your leg." "My leg, yes; my will, not even Zeus can conquer" (Discourses 1.1)
last: ONLY THE USE OF IMPRESSIONS IS WHOLLY MINE.

lines: A TYRANT LISTS WHAT HE CAN DO.
cards: A tyrant leans across the table and lists what he can do to you. Chains. Prison.
Worse. Epictetus stages this scene in the first discourse as a quick back-and-forth, almost like a comedy sketch. He wasn't writing from the safe side of power.
He grew up enslaved, with no say over his own body, and that gives his answers a particular weight. Notice who gets the funny lines. It isn't the man with the chains.

teach.b: Later in the first discourse, Epictetus runs through the hard things. I must die. Must I die groaning too?
I must be chained. Must I also whine about it? I must be exiled.
Does anyone stop me from going with a smile, cheerful and calm? Then the scene. Tell me your secrets, says the tyrant.
I won't; that's up to me. Then I'll chain you. What are you saying, man?

teach.h: MY LEG, YES. MY WILL, NOT EVEN ZEUS.
teach.b: My will, not even Zeus can overpower. I'll throw you in prison. You mean my little body.
I'll cut off your head. Well, when did I ever tell you mine was the only neck in the world that couldn't be cut?
The will he means is prohairesis, the power to choose, to judge, to assent or refuse. In the Discourses it names the part of you that's truly yours. A tyrant can move your body anywhere.

He can't make you agree that his threat is your harm. Later writers told a story that Epictetus' master once twisted his leg, and Epictetus calmly warned, you'll break it. When it broke, he said: didn't I tell you?
Nobody knows if that happened, and another ancient source says he was simply lame from illness. But the Discourses never ask anyone to pretend chains don't hurt.
They ask a narrower question: inside this constraint, what is still yours?
These, Epictetus says, are the things to rehearse, to write down every day, to practice. Not because a tyrant is coming. Because small chains come every week.

how: People practicing Stoicism often rehearse hard situations in advance and ask, inside each constraint, what still belongs to them: their choices, judgments and attention.

o: a strong will that always gets its own way
a legal right to own and keep your own property
the power to choose: the part of you no one can chain

games.q: not even zeus — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says chains don't hurt a wise person
he doesn't deny the chains. he asks what, inside them, is still yours.
the story of Epictetus' master breaking his leg is certain history
later writers told it; another ancient source says he was lame from illness.
which gives his answers to the tyrant a particular weight.

games.q: the tyrant says: I'll chain you. what does Epictetus answer?
o: you'll chain my leg. my will, not even Zeus can overpower.
games.why: the body can be chained; the power to choose and judge can't be forced, not even by Zeus.

practice: Bring to mind one constraint you're living inside right now, a job you can't leave yet, an illness, a tight budget, a body that won't do what it used to, and name it plainly.
Then ask Epictetus' question: inside this, what is still mine? How I speak, what I notice, what I agree to, where I put my attention: find one, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Prohairesis. The power to choose, to judge, to assent or refuse; chain the leg, but not even Zeus can overpower it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: choice, will, the power to choose, Epictetus' word for the self that's truly ours.

carryVoice: Your line: what is still yours. The leg can be chained; the will can't. Day three hundred ninety, done.

sources.ref: Origen, Against Celsus 7.53 (the leg story); Simplicius, Commentary on the Enchiridion (lameness)
